stem: Commerce is best described as
options: trade together with the aids to trade
the making of goods in factories
the extraction of raw materials from nature
buying and selling of goods only
explanation: Commerce covers trade (buying and selling) plus the services that help it, such as banking, transport, insurance, warehousing and advertising. Buying and selling alone is trade, which is only one part of commerce.

stem: Which hindrance of trade is removed by transport?
explanation: Goods are produced in one place and consumed in another; transport carries them across that distance, removing the hindrance of place. The hindrance of time is removed by warehousing, which stores goods until they are needed.

stem: Warehousing removes which hindrance of trade?
explanation: Goods are often produced in one season and consumed throughout the year. Warehouses store them until demand arises, bridging the gap of time. Distance (place) is the job of transport, not warehousing.

stem: A shopkeeper in Multan does not know that a new brand of ceiling fan exists in the market. The aid to trade that removes this hindrance is
explanation: Lack of information about goods is the hindrance of knowledge, which advertising removes by telling buyers what is available. Banking removes the hindrance of finance, not of information.

stem: Insurance is an aid to trade because it
options: removes every possible risk of fire, theft and accident from a business
supplies the trader with working capital
moves goods from producers to consumers
spreads the loss of a few among many who face the same risk
explanation: Insurance cannot prevent fire or theft; it collects premiums from many people facing a risk and compensates the few who actually suffer the loss. Saying it removes every risk is the common mistake: the risk remains, only its financial burden is shared.

stem: Trade carried on between buyers and sellers within the boundaries of one country is called
explanation: Home (internal) trade takes place within one country, for example between a Faisalabad mill and a Lahore shop. Entrepot and re-export trade both involve goods crossing national borders.

stem: Importing goods from one country in order to export them to another country is known as
explanation: Entrepot (re-export) trade means goods are imported, sometimes processed or repacked, and then sent on to a third country. Plain export trade sells home-produced goods abroad, not goods first brought in from outside.

stem: The main difference between wholesale and retail trade is that a wholesaler usually
options: sells for cash while retailers sell on credit
sells only imported goods to the public
deals in only one product while a retailer usually stocks many different products
sells in large quantities to retailers rather than to final consumers
explanation: A wholesaler buys in bulk from producers and sells in fairly large lots to retailers; the retailer then sells small quantities to consumers. Wholesalers often give credit to retailers, so the cash-versus-credit idea is false.

stem: Which of the following is a service provided by a wholesaler to manufacturers?
options: giving free after-sales repair service at each final consumer's home
selling small quantities to final consumers
buying goods in bulk and relieving them of storage
displaying goods in an attractive shop window
explanation: By placing large orders and holding the stock, the wholesaler frees manufacturers from storing finished goods and from finding many small buyers. Selling small quantities to consumers is the retailer's role.

stem: "Breaking the bulk" in trade refers to
options: dividing large consignments into smaller lots for resale
refusing to buy goods in large quantities
separating damaged or broken goods from a shipment before it is sold
explanation: Producers sell in bulk; wholesalers and retailers break these large quantities into lots small enough for the next buyer. It has nothing to do with damaged goods or machinery.

stem: A retailer is best described as
options: the last link between producers and consumers
a trader who sells only to other businesses
the first link between producers and wholesalers
an agent who never takes ownership of goods
explanation: The retailer sells directly to the final consumer, so he is the last link in the chain of distribution. Selling only to other businesses describes a wholesaler.

stem: A large shop with separate sections for clothing, furniture, toys and groceries under one roof and one management is a
explanation: A departmental store groups many departments in one building under a single management. A chain (multiple) store is the reverse arrangement: many branches in different places selling similar goods under one owner.

stem: Several shops in different cities, all owned by one firm, selling the same type of goods at uniform prices, are called
explanation: Multiple shops, also called chain stores, are branches of one business spread over different areas, with standard goods and prices. A departmental store is one large building with many sections, not many branches.

stem: A hawker who moves from street to street selling goods from a cart is an example of a
explanation: Itinerant retailers have no fixed place of business and move to reach customers, as hawkers and pedlars do. Fixed-shop retailers sell from permanent premises.

stem: In mail-order business, the seller and buyer mainly deal with each other through
options: face-to-face bargaining in a weekly market
auctions held at the seller's premises
catalogues, post or online orders with delivery to the buyer
a broker who keeps all the goods in his own warehouse until the buyer collects them
explanation: Mail-order sellers advertise through catalogues or online listings, receive orders by post or electronically, and deliver goods to the buyer; there is no personal contact at a shop. Bargaining in a market is a feature of fixed or periodic markets, not mail order.

stem: A supermarket is mainly characterised by
options: home delivery of every order by salesmen who visit customers each week
self-service, with customers picking goods and paying at checkouts
credit sales to all regular customers
sale of only one line of goods at high prices
explanation: In a supermarket, goods are displayed on open shelves, customers serve themselves and pay at a checkout; this keeps staff costs and prices low. Selling one line of goods describes a single-line or specialty shop.

stem: A written request from a buyer to a seller to supply stated goods on stated terms is
explanation: The buyer sends an order to say exactly what he wants and on what terms. A quotation goes the other way: from seller to buyer, stating prices and terms before any order is placed.

stem: The document a seller sends to a prospective buyer stating the prices and terms on which goods can be supplied is a
explanation: A quotation answers a buyer's enquiry with prices, discounts and delivery terms. Debit and credit notes adjust an amount after a sale has taken place.

stem: An invoice is a document that
options: is sent by the seller with details of goods sold and the amount due
gives the buyer legal ownership of goods while they are still at sea on a ship
is sent by the buyer to correct an earlier order
is issued by a bank to guarantee payment
explanation: An invoice lists the goods sent, quantities, prices, discounts and the total payable, and is prepared by the seller. A bank's guarantee of payment is a letter of credit, not an invoice.

stem: A pro forma invoice differs from an ordinary invoice because it
options: is prepared by the buyer's bank, not the seller
is sent before a sale is completed and does not demand payment
records the goods returned by the buyer to the seller after the sale is complete
is sent only after the buyer has fully paid
explanation: A pro forma invoice shows what an invoice would contain if the order were placed; it is used for quotations, advance payment or consignment, and it creates no debt. Goods returned are dealt with by a credit note.

stem: A seller finds that he undercharged a customer by Rs. 2,500 in an invoice. To correct this he should send the customer a
explanation: A debit note tells the buyer that his account has been debited with an extra amount, as when he was undercharged. A credit note is the opposite: it reduces the buyer's debt, as for an overcharge or goods returned.

stem: When a buyer returns damaged goods, the seller sends him a
explanation: Returned goods reduce what the buyer owes, so the seller credits the buyer's account and informs him with a credit note. A debit note would increase the buyer's debt.

stem: A document sent periodically by a supplier summarising all invoices, payments and returns for a customer, and showing the balance due, is a
explanation: A statement of account, usually sent monthly, summarises the transactions of the period and the closing balance. A delivery note only accompanies goods to list what has been delivered.

stem: The letters E. & O.E. printed at the foot of an invoice mean that
options: the invoice has been examined and officially endorsed
the goods have been sent at the buyer's own risk
the seller may correct any errors or omissions later
the price includes all export and other expenses
explanation: E. & O.E. stands for "errors and omissions excepted": the seller keeps the right to correct mistakes found in the invoice after it is sent. It says nothing about risk or expenses.

stem: A trade discount is allowed by a seller
options: only when the buyer pays before the due date
by the bank on early payment of a bill
on the list price, usually to traders buying for resale
only after the buyer has returned faulty goods and received a credit note
explanation: Trade discount is a reduction on the catalogue or list price given to traders, often for bulk buying, and is deducted on the invoice itself. A reduction for paying early is a cash discount.

stem: Goods listed at Rs. 40,000 are sold with 10 % trade discount and 5 % cash discount for payment within 10 days. If the buyer pays within 10 days, he pays
explanation: Trade discount first: 40,000 − 4,000 = 36,000. Cash discount on that: 5 % of 36,000 = 1,800, leaving 34,200. Taking 15 % of 40,000 at once gives 34,000, but the cash discount is calculated on the price after trade discount.

stem: Under an F.O.B. (free on board) contract, the seller bears the costs of the goods
options: including marine insurance up to the port of destination
until they reach the buyer's own warehouse in the importing country
only until they leave the seller's factory gate
until they are loaded on the ship at the port of shipment
explanation: In an F.O.B. price, the exporter pays all charges up to loading the goods on board; freight and insurance beyond that are the buyer's. Including insurance and freight to the destination port describes a C.I.F. price.

stem: A C.I.F. price quoted by a Karachi exporter includes
options: the cost of goods, insurance and freight to the port of destination
the cost of goods and inland carriage to Karachi port
the cost of goods only, at the exporter's factory
the cost of goods and the customs duty paid by the importer in his own country
explanation: C.I.F. means cost, insurance and freight: the exporter's price covers the goods plus their insurance and sea freight to the buyer's port. Import duty in the buyer's country is paid by the importer and is not part of C.I.F.

stem: A price that includes all expenses up to the buyer's own premises is called a
explanation: A franco price covers every cost of delivering goods to the buyer's door. A loco price is the opposite: the price at the seller's premises, with all carriage paid by the buyer.

stem: The document issued by a shipping company acknowledging receipt of goods on board and acting as a document of title is the
explanation: The bill of lading is the shipowner's receipt, the evidence of the contract of carriage and a document of title that can be transferred by endorsement. A mate's receipt is only a temporary receipt given at loading and later exchanged for the bill of lading.

stem: A mate's receipt is
options: a contract for hiring a whole ship for a voyage
the final document of title that the importer presents at the destination
a certificate issued by a chamber of commerce stating the country where goods were made
issued by the ship's officer on loading and later exchanged for a bill of lading
explanation: The mate (an officer of the ship) signs a receipt as goods are loaded; the exporter hands it to the shipping company to obtain the bill of lading. It is not itself the final document of title.

stem: A contract under which a trader hires a whole ship, or a large part of it, for a voyage or a period is a
explanation: A charter party is the agreement for hiring a ship. A bill of lading is used when goods are sent as ordinary cargo on a ship that also carries other shippers' goods.

stem: A document that certifies the country in which exported goods were produced is a
explanation: A certificate of origin, commonly issued by a chamber of commerce, proves where goods were made so that the importing country can apply the correct duty. A bill of entry is the importer's declaration to customs, not proof of origin.

stem: A letter of credit is mainly used in foreign trade because it
options: replaces the need for marine insurance on the cargo
assures the exporter that a bank will pay once the agreed documents are presented
gives the importer full legal ownership of the goods while they are still at sea on the ship
allows the exporter to avoid preparing any shipping documents
explanation: Under a letter of credit, the importer's bank undertakes to pay the exporter against specified documents such as the bill of lading and invoice, removing doubt about payment. It does not transfer ownership of goods; the bill of lading does that.

stem: An indent in foreign trade is
options: a permit issued by customs to release goods
a receipt issued by a warehouse for imported goods
an order placed by an importer with an agent to import goods for him
a list of all the goods sent by the exporter on the ship, prepared by its captain
explanation: An indent is an order sent through an indent house or agent who arranges the import on the importer's behalf. A list of goods sent with the ship is the ship's manifest, not an indent.

stem: In a closed indent, the importer
options: buys goods from the local wholesale market
names the particular manufacturer from whom the goods must be bought
pays the agent only after the imported goods have all been sold in the local market
leaves the choice of supplier entirely to the agent
explanation: A closed (specific) indent names the manufacturer, so the agent has no choice of supplier. An open indent leaves the choice of manufacturer to the agent.

stem: Before goods can be cleared from customs, an importer submits a statement of their description, quantity and value to the customs authorities. This document is the
explanation: The importer's declaration to customs for clearing imported goods is the bill of entry. The shipping bill is the matching document prepared by an exporter for goods leaving the country.

stem: A consular invoice is
options: a pro forma invoice prepared for a government tender
an invoice prepared by the customs office at the port of arrival
a bill sent by the shipping company for sea freight
an invoice certified by the importing country's consul in the exporting country
explanation: Some importing countries require the invoice to be certified by their consul stationed in the exporter's country, to check value and prevent false declarations. It is not a customs or freight document.

stem: A dock warrant is
options: a receipt given by the mate on loading cargo
a fine imposed for late removal of goods
a permit allowing a ship to enter the harbour
a document of title for goods stored in a dock warehouse
explanation: Dock authorities issue a dock warrant for goods kept in their warehouse; it can be transferred by endorsement, so the goods can be sold without moving them. The receipt given at loading is the mate's receipt.

stem: Barter means
options: exchanging goods directly for goods without using money
buying goods on credit for later payment
exchanging money of one country for another
explanation: Under barter, a farmer might exchange wheat for cloth with no money involved. Exchanging one currency for another is foreign exchange, not barter.

stem: The main difficulty of the barter system was the
options: very high rates of interest charged on all loans
lack of double coincidence of wants
explanation: Barter works only if each party wants exactly what the other offers, at the same time and in suitable amounts, which is rare. Money solved this by acting as a common medium of exchange.

stem: Mining, fishing and quarrying are examples of
explanation: Extractive industries take wealth directly from the land, water or air. Genetic industries instead breed and rear plants or animals, as in poultry farms and nurseries.

stem: A poultry farm that rears chicks for sale is an example of a
explanation: Genetic industries reproduce and multiply living things, such as poultry, cattle breeding and plant nurseries. Extractive industries remove natural resources without breeding them.

stem: Converting cotton into yarn and cloth in a Faisalabad mill is an example of
explanation: Manufacturing changes raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods with a higher value. Commerce only distributes goods once they are made.

stem: A broker differs from a factor in that a broker
options: keeps the goods and sells them in his own name
guarantees payment by the buyers for an extra commission
brings buyer and seller together without taking possession of the goods
buys the goods outright and resells them at a profit
explanation: A broker is a go-between who arranges contracts but does not hold the goods. A factor has possession of the goods and can sell them in his own name.

stem: An agent who, for an extra commission, guarantees his principal against bad debts from the buyers he finds is a
explanation: A del credere agent takes on the risk of buyers not paying and is paid an extra (del credere) commission for this guarantee. An ordinary broker gives no such guarantee.

stem: Under the balance of trade, a country has a deficit when
options: its banks lend more than they hold in deposits
its exports of goods exceed its imports of goods
its government spends more than it collects in taxes
its imports of goods exceed its exports of goods
explanation: The balance of trade compares visible exports and imports. An excess of imports over exports is a deficit; spending more than tax revenue is a budget deficit, a different idea.

stem: The balance of payments differs from the balance of trade because it
options: records only trade with neighbouring countries
includes only the exports and imports of goods
includes services, transfers and capital flows as well as goods
is prepared by commercial banks for their clients
explanation: The balance of trade covers goods only. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world, including services, remittances and capital movements.

stem: Commercial activity in Pakistan is most concentrated in Karachi chiefly because it
options: is the country's main seaport and industrial centre
lies at the centre of the Punjab plain
is close to the main coal mines of the country
is the federal capital of the country
explanation: Karachi's seaports handle most of Pakistan's foreign trade, and industry, banks and offices cluster around them. The federal capital is Islamabad, not Karachi.

stem: Sialkot is widely known for exporting
options: crude oil, natural gas and petroleum products
explanation: Sialkot's small and medium industries have long made footballs, other sports goods and surgical instruments for export. Rock salt comes mainly from the Salt Range, not Sialkot.

stem: Which factor most strongly influences the location of an industry that uses a heavy, bulky raw material which loses much of its weight in processing?
options: nearness to the source of the raw material
explanation: If a raw material loses weight in processing, carrying it far is wasteful, so such industries, for example sugar mills near cane fields, locate close to the raw material. Nearness to consumers matters more for goods that gain weight or are perishable after manufacture.

stem: Gwadar port is located in the province of
explanation: Gwadar is on the Makran coast of Balochistan. Pakistan's other major ports, Karachi Port and Port Qasim, are both in Sindh.

stem: A commission agent is paid
options: interest on the money he lends to buyers
a percentage of the value of the business he arranges
the whole profit made on goods he sells
a fixed monthly salary regardless of sales
explanation: A commission agent works for a principal and receives commission, a percentage of the sales or purchases he makes. Keeping the whole profit is what a merchant who buys on his own account does.

stem: A large retail shop that sells only one kind of product, such as shoes, in many styles and sizes is a
explanation: A single-line store concentrates on one line of goods and offers wide choice within it. A departmental or general store sells many unrelated lines.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the aids to trade?
explanation: Banking, warehousing, advertising, insurance and transport help trade take place, so they are aids to trade. Manufacturing is part of industry: it makes the goods that trade then distributes.

stem: Selling goods to buyers in other countries is called
explanation: Export trade sends home-produced goods to foreign buyers. Import trade is buying goods from abroad.

stem: The main function of banking as an aid to trade is to remove the hindrance of
explanation: Banks provide loans, overdrafts and means of payment, solving the trader's shortage of funds. The hindrance of place is removed by transport.

stem: A retailer who sells from a small shop in a residential street, often giving credit to known customers, is a
explanation: A local general store stocks daily necessities near customers' homes and often gives credit to regular buyers. A hawker has no fixed shop.

stem: The term "cash on delivery" means that
options: the buyer pays when the goods are handed over to him
the seller pays the carrier's charges in full
the buyer pays in advance before the goods are sent
the buyer pays three months after receiving the goods and the invoice
explanation: With cash on delivery, payment is collected when the goods are delivered. Paying before goods are sent is payment in advance.

stem: Goods listed at Rs. 80,000 carry trade discounts of 10 % and then a further 5 %. What is the invoice price?
explanation: Successive discounts are applied one after another: 80,000 × 0.90 = 72,000, then 72,000 × 0.95 = 68,400. Adding them to 15 % gives 68,000, which is wrong because the second discount is taken on the reduced price.

stem: A delivery note is sent
options: by a bank, confirming payment to the seller
by customs, allowing goods to leave the port
before the order, quoting prices and terms
with the goods, listing what has been delivered
explanation: A delivery note travels with the goods; the buyer checks and signs it as proof of receipt. Prices and terms before an order appear in a quotation.

stem: Goods sent by air are accompanied by a receipt and contract of carriage called the
explanation: The airline or its agent issues an airway bill as a receipt and evidence of the contract of carriage; unlike a bill of lading, it is normally not a document of title. A bill of lading is used for goods sent by sea.

stem: An importer pays an indent house to arrange imports. The indent house earns
options: interest on the importer's bank deposit
a commission on the value of goods imported
the customs duty paid on the goods
explanation: An indent house acts as agent and is rewarded by commission. Customs duty goes to the government and freight to the carrier.

stem: An auctioneer sells goods by
options: keeping goods on display in a chain of shops
quoting a fixed price that cannot change
inviting bids in public and selling to the highest bidder
explanation: At an auction, buyers bid against each other and the goods go to the highest bid. A fixed, non-negotiable price is a one-price shop's method.

stem: In an open indent, the agent
options: is free to buy from any suitable manufacturer
sells the importer's goods in a foreign market
pays customs duty on behalf of the exporter
must buy from the manufacturer named by the importer
explanation: An open indent states the goods, price limits and terms but leaves the choice of supplier to the agent. Naming the supplier makes it a closed indent.

stem: Which aid to trade brings buyers' attention to new products?
explanation: Advertising informs and persuades buyers about goods and services. Insurance only covers risks of loss.

stem: A Lahore firm imports machinery from China and sells it to a buyer in Afghanistan without using it. This is an example of
explanation: Goods brought into a country and sent on to a third country are re-exported, which is entrepot trade. It is not simple export trade, because the machinery was not produced in Pakistan.
